newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Hounded by critics, Swiss hunt historical truth.
newsitem.headline: Hounded by critics, Swiss hunt historical truth.

text.p: Switzerland faces a historic challenge to lay bare the fate of Holocaust victims' accounts in Swiss banks and to re-examine its complex wartime ties with Nazi Germany.

The task at hand won fresh urgency last week when a World Jewish Congress official accused Switzerland of immorally stripping Holocaust victims of their wealth by striking a secret deal in 1949 ceding Poles' unclaimed wartime assets to Warsaw.

Switzerland denies the confidential accord -- which came to light in a previously unpublished exchange of letters attached to a compensation pact for nationalised Swiss property -- let it keep the property of Poles killed in Nazi death camps.
But it underscored the political importance of settling once and for all a controvery that has drawn international attention and damaged Switzerland's reputation as a financial centre.

"The search for the wealth of Jews who were killed and expelled in the thousand-year (Nazi) Reich is of the greatest importance to us," federal energy minister Moritz Leuenberger was quoted on Sunday as telling a meeting of Jewish groups.

The Sonntags Zeitung newspaper said he acknowledged that Switzerland "for years shied away from admitting that our willingness and ability to defend ourselves (against Hilter) did not alone save our country from war and destruction".

Younger Swiss historians say it was not just the outgunned Swiss army that kept Hitler from crushing his neutral Alpine neighbours, but also broad Swiss economic collaboration with Germany that helped finance the Nazi war effort.
This included huge purchases of gold from stores the Nazis looted from the countries and peoples they conquered.

This sceptical historical view and foreign accusations that the Swiss just looked on and profitted from Nazi terror in Europe have angered many Swiss, who see it as an attack on their parents and grandparents, known as the "active duty generation".
They say foreign critics tend to forget that tiny neutral Switzerland was surrounded by fascist powers who were choking off its ability to conduct an independent foreign policy.

Sonntags Blick columnist Frank Meyer said those who deserve criticism were the captains of industry glad to see Hitler smash leftists and trade unions, the army officers convinced Hitler would win and the politicians who saw democracy as outdated.
"International criticism targets these groups, cliques and persons who, out of greed for profits and power, were all too willing to help the Nazis, the enemy of the world," he wrote.

Switzerland is operating at three levels to investigate claims, voiced last week at an emotional hearing held by U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato, that Swiss banks stonewalled families of Holocaust victims seeking unclaimed assets in Switzerland.

A banking ombudsman is coordinating nearly 1,000 claims for any accounts that may have escaped two prior sweeps of banks' records. A separate panel formed by Swiss banks and Jewish groups in May is about to hire auditors to comb banks' files.
"The biggest difficulty we face is very simple -- all this happened 50 years or more ago," the panel's chairman, former U.S. central bank chief Paul Volcker, said last week.
"I see no indications at this point of difficulty from a lack of cooperation from either the Swiss banks or the Swiss government," he told reporters.

Parliament is also set to give final approval in December for a panel of historians and experts empowered to lift Swiss banking secrecy and probe the fate of any Holocaust accounts as part of a sweeping review of Switzerland's wartime role.

Swiss banks have never disputed they were a popular refuge for the wealth of European Jews fearing Nazi persecution after Hitler came to power in Germany in 1933. Many were drawn by Switzerland's strict bank secrecy and neutral status.
But banks reject claims by the World Jewish Congress that they may still be sitting on billions of dollars in such assets.
